applied.fact: Camp location, elevation and camping rules
Camp location, elevation and camping rules
Camp location, elevation and camping rules

before.beta: The easiest way up Ives Peak is a scramble. The standard approach follows the Pacific Crest Trail / Goat Rocks crest, which runs close to the peak's western slopes, then leaves the crest to climb the northeast side to the summit; this is unroped class 2-3 talus/scree, not a technical rock or ice route. A 2026 ski-mountaineering trip report (climberkyle.com) that circled the peak describes the ridge north of the summit as rocky and wind-scoured, with a short loose ('choss') section near the col, and notes lingering snow on the peak's flanks into early summer.
before.face: Northeast side of Ives Peak, reached along the Goat Rocks crest between Old Snowy Mountain and the summit
before.approach: Start at the Snowgrass Trailhead (aka "Berry Patch," elev. ~4,600 ft), reached via FR-21 (Johnson Creek Road) off US-12 about 3 miles west of Packwood. From the trailhead, follow the Snowgrass Trail #96 south then east through dense forest; the trail drops slightly (~75 ft) to cross Goat Creek on a footbridge/plank crossing around the 2-mile mark (only real water crossing on the approach, and a reliable water source — top off here or at the creeks in upper Snowgrass Flat). Continue climbing through subalpine forest and meadow to Lower Snowgrass Flat, then Upper Snowgrass Flat at roughly 6,400 ft (about 4 miles / ~1,800 ft gain from the trailhead) — a broad, popular wildflower meadow with good camping and multiple small creeks (last dependable water before the ridge). From Upper Snowgrass Flat, continue about 0.3–0.5 mile further to the junction with the Pacific Crest Trail at roughly 6,700–7,100 ft (~4.3 miles in). Leave the PCT here and head off-trail to the northeast, ascending talus and scree with no defined tread (occasional cairns) toward the low col on the ridge crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak — expect loose, unconsolidated talus that shifts underfoot; test holds and footing carefully. From the col, follow the ridge crest or a line just south of it (Class 2) over a rounded intermediate high point toward Ives' northwest ridge. At the base of the true summit block, a boot path threads up scree toward a notch between two rock outcrops; above the notch is a short cliff band — downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge (Class 2) to gain the upper south face, then scramble roughly 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock and up easy terrain to the 7,920-ft summit. Snowfields commonly linger on the approach slopes and in the col well into July (this basin can hold 25–40 ft of winter snowpack), so an ice axe is worth carrying for early/mid-season attempts on the traverse.

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Trail, the PCT junction and the Old Snowy to Ives col
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Snowgrass trailhead, also called Berry Patch, at about 4,600 ft, reached by forest road off the highway west of Packwood. Follow Snowgrass Trail #96 south then east through dense forest; it drops slightly to cross Goat Creek on a plank crossing around the 2-mile mark, which is the only real water crossing and a reliable source. Climb through subalpine forest and meadow to Lower and then Upper Snowgrass Flat at roughly 6,400 ft, about 4 miles in — a broad wildflower meadow with good camping and small creeks, the last dependable water before the ridge. Continue a further 0.3 to 0.5 mile to the PCT junction at roughly 6,700-7,100 ft. Leave the PCT and head off-trail northeast, ascending talus and scree with no defined tread and only occasional cairns, toward the low col on the crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak. The talus is unconsolidated and shifts underfoot. Snowfields linger on the approach slopes and in the col well into July — this basin can hold 25 to 40 ft of winter snowpack — so an axe is worth carrying for early and mid-season attempts.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jul through mid-Sep, once the crest and shaded gullies have melted out
hazards: Loose, unconsolidated talus and scree with higher consequence on the descent
Chossy volcanic andesite on the summit south face
An exposed narrow ledge traverse below the summit, reached by downclimbing
Lingering snowfields and a moat crossing near the col into July
Off-trail route-finding with no maintained summit path
Exposure to afternoon thunderstorms on an open crest
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL BETWEEN OLD SNOWY AND IVES IS THE ARRIVAL, AND YOU GET TO IT BY LEAVING A TRAIL, NOT BY FOLLOWING ONE.

Leave the PCT at the junction area, roughly 6,700-7,100 ft, and go off-trail NORTHEAST up talus. There is no tread. Occasional cairns are the only marks. If you are still on maintained trail you have not started the route.

YOU KNOW YOU ARE AT THE COL BECAUSE YOU ARE BETWEEN TWO PEAKS at about 7,250 ft — Old Snowy behind you, Ives ahead. A high point on one side only is not the col.

THE BUMP IS THE TRAP AND IT IS COUNTABLE: from the col the ridge crosses a ROUNDED INTERMEDIATE HIGH POINT before you reach the true summit block. THAT BUMP IS NOT THE SUMMIT. If you have not passed one rounded bump, you have not reached the summit block, whatever the ground in front of you looks like.

THE BASE OF THE SCRAMBLE IS A NOTCH BETWEEN TWO ROCK OUTCROPS, reached by a boot path up scree. And here is the test that settles it beyond doubt, because it is the opposite of what you expect at a summit block: ABOVE THE NOTCH IS A SHORT CLIFF BAND, AND THE ROUTE GOES DOWN FIRST. You downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge to gain the upper south face, then scramble about 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock to easy ground and the summit.

SO: IF THE LINE IN FRONT OF YOU ONLY GOES UP, YOU ARE AT THE WRONG NOTCH. Having to lose a little height at the notch is the confirmation.

DESCENT FINDING WORTH MAKING BEFORE YOU START: dropping straight southwest off the col into the basin is faster and is the loosest ground on the mountain. Traversing back over Old Snowy and down its established south-ridge path avoids the worst of it.

waypoints.name: Snowgrass Flat Trailhead (Trail #96)
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk (no fee); Northwest Forest Pass or National Park Pass required to park, with an overflow lot at nearby Berry Patch Trailhead.

waypoints.name: Goat Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford of Goat Creek on the Snowgrass Trail in forest cover; a reliable water source about 2 miles in.

waypoints.name: Lower Snowgrass Flat / Lily Basin Trail (#86) junction
waypoints.note: Established campsites near the Lily Basin Trail junction; a spring at the head of Snowgrass Creek (about a quarter mile off-trail) is the last dependable water before the ridge.

waypoints.name: Pacific Crest Trail junction
waypoints.note: Snowgrass Trail meets the PCT; head north toward Old Snowy Mountain to reach the Ives approach ridge.

waypoints.name: Old Snowy - Ives col
waypoints.note: Saddle between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak where the north ridge route onto Ives begins; also the top of the Class 1-2 northwest ridge used on the descent.

waypoints.name: Southwest face ramp traverse
waypoints.note: Drop off the ridge crest onto a loose ramp and traverse roughly 40 ft climber's right below the summit cliff; exposed Class 3 terrain, loose underfoot.

waypoints.name: Ives Peak summit
waypoints.note: Broad rocky true summit (7,920+ ft) with views of Mt. Adams, Mt. Rainier, and the McCall Glacier on the northeast face.

weather.typical: Highly exposed alpine crest weather that can change rapidly with little shelter along the ridge
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are common during the July-August window

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained exposure along the narrow Goat Rocks crest with unroped Class 3 moves over loose rock; a slip risks a long fall, and rockfall from parties above is a real concern, hence helmet use

avalanche.zone: NWAC South Cascades forecast zone (regional coverage; no zone specific to Ives Peak/Goat Rocks itself)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel on the standard NE Slopes/crest scramble route; the McCall Glacier lies below the ridge on the NE flank and is generally avoided by staying on rock, though traverse variants toward Old Snowy can pass near its moat/edge
